title.en: Why свежий changes with its noun

summary.en: Treat the adjective ending as a clue to the noun beside it.

body.en:
From season 1, episodes 1 and 2.

Morning life at the inn is full of describing words that shift their endings to match the noun beside them: **горячий чай** (*hot tea*), **свежая краска** (*fresh paint*), **чистое окно** (*clean window*), and **свежие утренние булочки** (*fresh morning buns*).

Russian adjectives agree with the noun they describe in grammatical gender, number and case. Even though **свежий**, **свежая** and **свежие** all carry the core meaning *fresh*, the ending mirrors the noun: feminine singular **краска** takes **свежая**, while plural **полотенца** and **булочки** take **свежие**.

Agreement follows the grammatical gender of the Russian word, not real-world biology: **чай** is masculine (**горячий чай**), **комната** is feminine (**чистая комната**), and **дерево** is neuter (**старое дерево**).

On replay, spot the noun first and then listen to the ending on the describing word beside it—the two endings work together as one pair.
